blocks.text: it’s time for The Weekend Read , your Saturday digest of all the long-form pieces you might have missed during the week.

First off, there’s our in-depth cover story with Andrew Scott, in which he muses on life, death and his latest film ‘Elsinore’, then, perhaps our most divisive review yet: The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping . Speaking of divisive, we also have our columnist Baz Bamigboye’s thoughts on the casting of Robert Pattinson as Bond.
Then, we have a look at the huge video game launch Grand Theft Auto VI and a review of Brad Pitt-starrer The Further Mid-Adventures of Cliff Booth.
Click on the below to find out more!

Andrew Scott Talks Life, Death & ‘Elsinore’ In Elsinore, Andrew Scott plays real-life actor Ian Charleson — a man for whom the phrase ‘rage against the dying of the light’ might have been written. In 1989, when Charleson discovers he’s facing his own imminent death from AIDS-related illness, he’s offered his dream role, and deciding he’d “rather die of Hamlet than AIDS,” he takes to the stage in the ultimate act of defiance. Scott has been acting since he was eight years old. Ever since his mother, Nora, who was an art teacher, encouraged him to act as a way to get past shyness and a childhood lisp. A successful stage career followed, along with Spielberg’s TV miniseries Band of Brothers , a BAFTA-winning Sherlock role as Moriarty and a villain in the Bond film Spectre , among other things. But, it was, of course, Scott’s ‘hot priest’ in Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag that shot him to major stardom — it seemed everyone, including the critics, craved the forbidden fruit of his clergyman character. After that came Andrew Haigh’s All of Us Strangers opposite Paul Mescal and double Emmy nominations for the miniseries Ripley . Under Simon Stone ’s direction and with Stephen Beresford ’s screenplay, Scott, who also serves as a producer, is joined by Olivia Colman as Ian’s physician Dr. Margaret Johnson, Billie Piper and Matthew Beard as Ian’s friends Patsy Pollock and Sean Mathias, Johnny Flynn as Hamlet director Richard Eyre , and such greats as Juliet Stevenson, who actually worked with Charleson in multiple stage productions, including The Taming of the Shrew in 1979. blocks.text: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Review Image Credit: Lionsgate Not so long ago, the old it’s-funny-because-it’s-true joke about soap operas was that people in soap operas never seemed to watch soap operas. But now that reality shows have all but taken over that space, the function of soaps has evaporated almost entirely, while “unscripted TV” has absorbed all of its clichés. When it first appeared in 2012, The Hunger Games seemed fresh and even satirical; now, though, it just feels tired, and this sixth lackluster offering raises only one serious question: Hasn’t anyone forced to take part in a violent dystopic game show ever seen a violent dystopic game show before? Aha, you might say. This is a prequel , taking place a full 24 years before the original. True, the citizens of Panem have only had to put up with 49 editions of the Hunger Games thus far, but, leaving aside the ancient art of combat-for-entertainment explored in both Gladiator movies, in our world the idea of films pitting humans against humans has been around since 1932’s The Most Dangerous Game — and we’ve seen it all before, even if they haven’t. True, the target audience for this wasn’t alive for Logan’s Run (1976), or The Running Man (1987), and would have certainly missed Bong Joon Ho’s little-seen Snowpiercer (2013). But most would have been around for Edgar Wright’s recent Running Man remake, which this film most closely resembles. Read the full review here

blocks.text: Baz Bamigboye’s Analysis On Robert Pattinson As Bond Image Credit: Amazon MGM Studios A wise movie-world person of my acquaintance who has resided in these British isles long enough to understand the customs of the country shook their head when they heard that Robert Pattinson had been officially cast to play Ian Fleming’s James Bond in the 007 reboot that Denis Villeneuve is in pre-production to direct. They intoned: “Bond is mysterious. Bond creates the stars. The stars don’t create Bond,” then added for good measure, “For f*ck’s sake!” While I don’t think it’s the right thing for reinventing Bond, my sense is that Pattinson will be good, though I don’t think it’s hardly fresh to cast a 40-year-old movie star. blocks.text: Grand Theft Auto VI’s Shattering Launch Image Credit: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty Images Taylor Swift and AI investment have proven to be big boosts to the U.S. economy in the recent years. Yet, come Thursday, the mayhem-packed Grand Theft Auto VI is going to be the heavy hitter with record- breaking stats and a possibly legislative long-tail that could truly change the game. Or, as they’ve been saying repeatedly this midterms-mocking season on Comedy Central’s South America (a.k.a. South Park ): “If you ask me, this whole country has gone to sh*t …But hopefully things will get better in November. That’s when Grand Theft Auto VI comes out.” Exceeding $1.65 billion in pre-order sales, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tracker, the first new game in the GTA video game franchise in 13 years is already the most successful entertainment industry launch ever. ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Review Image Credit: Everett Collection Whenever people ask me what my favorite movie of all time is I always have a hard time answering that impossible question . But if you want to know my favorite of the past 10 years or so it’s simple. I can easily say Quentin Tarantino ‘s 2019 Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. So any idea of a sequel to this L.A. masterpiece set in 1969 that starred Leonardo DiCaprio and Brad Pitt — as Rick Dalton, a movie star who has seen better days, and Cliff Booth his stuntman/sidekick, respectively — has big shoes to fill following a movie that received 10 Oscar nominations and won two including Best Supporting Actor for Pitt. In my opinion it should also have won Best Picture and Director for Tarantino but I digress. Read the full review here
